newsitem.title: USA: U.S. farmers increase push for ethanol tax break.
newsitem.headline: U.S. farmers increase push for ethanol tax break.

text.p: U.S. farm groups are stepping up pressure on Congressional leaders to keep a tax break for ethanol producers off the Federal budget's chopping block.

House Ways and Means Chairman Bill Archer of Texas has repeatedly said he wants to repeal the tax break to help balance the budget, while farmers want to keep it as a production incentive at a time ethanol use appears to be finally attracting the interest of major automakers.

Under present law, producers of ethanol who blend it with gasoline can claim a 5.4 cent per gallon exemption on an 18.4 cents a gallon excise tax as part of a measure approved by Congress to extend through the year 2000.
In the United States, ethanol is made mainly from corn.
In a letter this week, 33 farm groups told House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Minority Leader Dick Gephardt that lifting the tax incentives would hurt the farm economy.

"I believe this is the largest collection of agricultural groups to send a joint letter in 15 or 16 years," Eric Vaughn, president of the Renewable Fuels Association in Washingon, said of the June 2 letter.

The letter, initiated by the American Farm Bureau Federation and signed by groups including the Renewable Fuels Association and the National Corn Growers Association, argued that the tax subsidy provided 192,000 jobs and increased farm income by $4.5 billion a year.
"Numerous studies have demonstrated that the federal ethanol program is good for the economy, for the environment, and for farmers and rural communities," the letter said.

Farm groups are worried that Archer, a Texas Republican, could succeed with his push to cut the ethanol tax break this year because of the retirement of Senator Robert Dole, the former majority leader who had backed the ethanol subsidy.

The letter coincided with an announcement by Ford Motor Co on June 3 that it plans to make 250,000 pickup trucks with "flexible fuel" engines that can run on both ethanol and gasoline, with the first models available in Fall, 1998.
The announcement was a welcome surprise to the ethanol industry. Vaughn said the farm groups were unaware of the car company's plans when they sent the letter.
"If all those cars were run on ethanol and averaged 15,000 miles a year, that would be approximately 1.6 billion gallons of ethanol a year," Vaughn said.
Chrysler Corporation is expected to announce on June 10 its own alternative-fuel vehicle as a flexible fuel minivan that would run on an "E-85" blend -- 85 percent ethanol and 15 percent gasoline.
The model is expected to be available in the 1998 model year, which starts this September, auto industry consultant Michael Robinet of CSM Forecasting said this week.
